bib.title: Skill-based Agentic Evaluation for Real-time Data Science Tasks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Skill-based Agentic Evaluation for Real-Time Data Science Tasks" (the PDF title line reads "Skill-based Agentic Evaluation for Data Science Tasks"). Authors: Aniruddha Tamhane, Raghavendra Addanki, Ayushi Aggarwal, Aditya Bansal, Rui Wang, Charles Menguy, Swati Jain, all at Adobe. It is arXiv:2609.16487v1 [cs.AI], dated 15 Sep 2026, and marked "A PREPRINT". There is no venue. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/tamhane-2026-skill-based-agentic-evaluation-real.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 45,553 characters across all 11 pages: the body, limitations, ethics statement, references and Appendix A. Nothing was skipped. Figure 1 is a flow diagram, and only its caption extracted as text. I also read note 05 (frontmatter, "Three judge shapes", "Decompose hard criteria", "Known biases") and note 06 ("Grade the outcome by state"). I only grepped note 07.

TARGET NOTE FIT
- Note 05 does not cite this paper. Its closest section is "Decompose hard criteria", which holds claim-by-claim grounding and completeness checks, G-Eval, CoVe and the Arike quote-extraction monitor. The "Reference-guided" row of "Three judge shapes" is also relevant.
- What 05 covers: decomposition into claims, and reference-guided judging with its failure mode (paraphrases accepted, master keys).
- What 05 lacks: a reference that is code recomputed at eval time, and factoid-level precision and recall with matched, omitted and hallucinated sets logged. It also lacks any evidence on judge agreement with a weak or missing reference.
- A better primary home is 06-evaluating-agents.md, "Grade the outcome by state, not by words". Its Data/SQL row says "Query result matches the reference result (not the reference SQL text)". This paper extends that row to live, drifting data. 05 should get a short sharpens-style pointer.
- Note 07 already covers FActScore and SAFE claim-by-claim checking, so the factoid half is partly covered. The new part is code-as-reference.

CORE CLAIM: When the correct answer changes with the data, store the reference as an executable function that is run at eval time against the same live data the agent saw. Then have an LLM judge split both the response and that computed reference into atomic claims, match them one to one, and score precision, recall and accuracy.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Ground-truth-as-code gets higher judge-to-human agreement than a natural-language reference or no reference.
 - number: MCC 0.427 vs 0.331 vs -0.379
 - setup: 53 comparable test cases of 55. Skill under test is an in-house ML skill (ML-goal identification and dataset discovery), run on a synthetic database. Harness is Claude Code and the model is Claude Sonnet 4.6, used for both skill and judge. Reference is three expert annotators. One run per configuration, no intervals reported.
 - quote: "Relative to a natural-language ground-truth baseline, ground-truth-as-code improves the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)... by29% (0.427 vs. 0.331) and reduces token cost per test case by 16%, while a self-directed baseline lacking explicit ground truth is anti-correlated with human judgment (MCC =−0.379 )."
 - where: p.2, Introduction; Table 3, p.5
2. Table 3 in full.
 - number: Baseline-1 (No GT): MCC -0.379, P 0.238, R 0.200, F1 0.217, ~70k tokens per test case. Baseline-2 (NL GT): 0.331, 0.561, 0.920, 0.697, 29.2k. GT-as-code: 0.427, 0.568, 1.000, 0.724, ~24.6k.
 - quote: "Baseline-2: NL GT 0.331 0.561 0.920 0.697 29.2k" and "GT-as-code (ours) 0.427 0.568 1.000 0.724∼24.6k"
 - where: p.5, Table 3
3. A judge with no supplied reference grades the skill against its own claims.
 - number: MCC -0.379, about 70k tokens per test case
 - quote: "Baseline-1 consistently evaluated each response only against the final-answer checks explicitly declared as final checks in the skill under test; it never formulated an alternate pathway to compute the ground truth and thus never accessed the real-time data."
 - setup: it used the harness's built-in skill-creator skill, prompted to devise its own correctness criteria.
 - where: p.6, Section 5.1
4. The natural-language reference failed by over-specifying inputs, which added extra factoids.
 - number: none
 - quote: "Baseline-2 did invoke the correct API function, but over-specified some of its input parameters; the resulting reference carried extra factoids that occasionally confounded the LLM judge, depressing precision"
 - where: p.6
5. The human labels are reliable by the paper's own measure.
 - number: Gwet's AC2 0.931 (factoid level) and 0.883 (all dimensions), against a 0.667 threshold
 - quote: "Prevalence-adjusted Gwet's AC2 clears the 0.667 acceptability threshold at both the factoid level (0.931) and the stacked-dimension level (0.883)"
 - setup: three domain-expert annotators after a calibration round, with live-data access. They used a 5-point Likert per factoid and a 5-point Likert on three qualitative dimensions.
 - where: p.5
6. Metric definitions: factoids are matched one to one with no partial credit, so the scorecard lists hallucinated and omitted claims.
 - number: none
 - quote: "Each match is a binary decision (no partial credit), so a matched factoid is unambiguously correct and an unmatched one unambiguously wrong" and "each scorecard logs Fr \ Frg (hallucinated claims) and Fg \ Frg (omitted facts) verbatim"
 - where: p.4, Sections 3.4 and 3.5
 - extra detail: the response is extracted unconditioned and the reference is extracted conditioned on the user query. Accuracy is |Frg| / (|Fg| + |Fr| - |Frg|). Scores are rescaled to 0-9.
7. The worked example gives a concrete scorecard.
 - number: |Fr|≈14, |Fg|≈12, |Frg|≈5, so P≈0.36, R≈0.42, A≈0.24, which are 3.2, 3.8 and 2.1 on the 0-9 scale. Overall is 5.1.
 - quote: "P= 514 ≈0.36, R= 512 ≈0.42, A= 514+12−5 = 521 ≈0.24."
 - setup: one financial-vertical test case. The agent chose the wrong dataset bundle, used a utilization heuristic for the target, and gave no leakage warning.
 - where: p.11, Appendix A.5; Tables 4 and 5
8. The synthetic benchmark is built to catch lexical-overlap shortcuts.
 - number: 353,330 event records, 30,000 profiles, 82 catalog entries, 26-week window, three verticals
 - setup: a Poisson-DAG generator, a stage sandbox behind the same APIs, five decoy types, and 2-week bundles to trap agents that ignore recency.
 - quote: "Satisfying a ground-truth function requires identifyingall threedatasets of a bundle—events, profiles, and catalog—so any decoy selection incurs a precision penalty."
 - where: p.5, Section 4; Table 1

LIMITS
Stated by the authors:
- The same model, Claude Sonnet 4.6, powers both the skill and the judge. They say "a systematic study that varies the judge model independently of the skill model remains valuable future work."
- The method assumes the code is correct and complete. "If Gi omits a relevant sub-query or computes it incorrectly, the resulting factoid-level metrics will misjudge the agent accordingly."
- Writing the code costs more expert effort than writing a natural-language reference, and auto-generating it is untested.
- The natural-language baseline should be re-run with stronger models (Opus, GPT-5.5).
- The token-efficiency claim needs testing on other harnesses with different caching.
- The scope is limited to tasks whose answers can be computed from accessible data APIs.

Unstated:
- n=53, one run, and no confidence interval on MCC, so the 0.096 absolute gap is untested for significance.
- Only the judge is validated against humans. The drift-resistance claim itself is never tested, for example by re-running after the data changes.
- It covers one skill, two sub-tasks, and a synthetic database.
- Human labels came from three annotators, and the paper does not say how they were combined into one PASS/FAIL.
- The PASS/FAIL threshold on the 0-9 exec_score is not given.
- Annotators saw the ground truth, so human labels are not independent of it.
- The tone, coverage and conciseness judge is not separately validated.
- Token cost is reported as approximate ("~").

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES
- Table 3 shows precision of 0.568 against 0.561, a gap too small to carry the claim that the natural-language reference "depress[ed] precision". The real gain is recall (0.920 to 1.000) and MCC. The text still concludes "The most precise and token-efficient ground-truth computation".
- GT-as-code recall is 1.000 with precision 0.568. The judge therefore passes every case humans passed, but also passes many that humans failed. This leniency is not discussed.
- Appendix A.2 says that in the benchmark the function "retrieves and formats the reference specification for the case". The reference is therefore effectively a stored spec, while the "recomputes from live data" behaviour is only asserted: "the same code-based interface generalizes to reference functions that recompute the answer from live data".
- 55 cases are reported, 53 are "comparable", and the 2 dropped are not explained.
- The self-bias argument ("little room for stylistic self-preference") is asserted and not measured.
- The arithmetic in the worked example checks out.

BUILDS ON
- FActScore (Min et al., 2023) and SAFE (Wei et al., 2024) for atomic-fact scoring.
- Jafari et al. (2026) and Fan et al. (2025) for factoid precision and recall.
- Text-to-SQL execution accuracy: WikiSQL/Seq2SQL (Zhong et al., 2017), Spider (Yu et al., 2018), BIRD (Li et al., 2023), Spider 2.0 (Lei et al., 2024).
- LLM-as-judge: Zheng et al. (2023), Gu et al. (2024), Szymanski et al. (2025), and Agent-as-a-Judge (Zhuge et al., 2024).
- RAGAS (Es et al., 2023) and ARES (Saad-Falcon et al., 2023) as adjacent RAG-evaluation work.
- LiveBench (White et al., 2024), PolyBench (Arora et al., 2026), Margatina et al. (2023) and Shi et al. (2025) for drift and contamination.
- The problem framing comes from Chen et al. (2026a, arXiv:2506.08800), who identify the lack of time-varying ground truth as an open challenge.
- Agent benchmarks: GAIA, DSGym, KramaBench, DABstep, DSAEval.

CODE: the paper has no code. The one reusable artifact is the call format in Appendix A.2 (p.10): get_ground_truth_string(idx=0, gt_keys=['ml_goal_type', 'target_variable', 'expected_datasets', 'input_variables', 'target_mapping_function', 'observation_window_days', 'outcome_window_days', 'failure_modes'])

FIGURES
- Figure 1 (p.4): "Evaluation flow for a single test case τi = (Ui, Gi, E, C). Both the skill response ri and the ground-truth output gi are produced at evaluation time against live data. Factoids are extracted from each, matched semantically, and aggregated into a per-test-case scorecard."
- It is the figure candidate. It shows the parallel run-skill and execute-G paths, then extract, match and score. It is faster to read than the prose.
- The Appendix A worked-example table (Tables 4 and 5) could carry a small P/R/A example for note 05, but the Figure 1 pipeline is the better teaching figure.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction is clean, apart from some run-together words in the title and headings and the garbled fractions in the appendix formulas ("514" means 5/14).
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
- The title differs between the extracted title line and the filename ("Real-Time" is missing from the PDF title line).
- The paper is a September 2026 single-organisation preprint with no peer review. Treat its numbers as a small, uncontrolled agreement study, and cite it with n=53, a single run and the same-model caveat.
- I wrote no files and made no edits.
